h1: Opening a brewpub in a country you did not grow up in
title: Opening a Brewpub in a New Country | Craft Beer School
desc: What changes when you open a brewpub in a country you did not grow up in: licences, suppliers, water, staff and customers, in the order to tackle them.
teaser: A brewpub abroad fails on the dull things first: the licence sequence, the water report and a landlord who has never heard of a brewhouse.
standfirst: Opening in a country you did not grow up in means learning three systems at once: the rules, the supply chain and the drinkers. This guide puts them in a workable order.
sections: Start with the rules, not the recipe

Every country licenses alcohol differently. Many split the rules again by state, province or city. Most share the same chain of approvals: a registered company, approved premises, a production licence, a sales or on-trade licence and an excise or duty registration. The order and the names change from place to place.

Before you spend on equipment, find out whether a foreigner or a foreign-owned company may hold the licence at all. Some places require a local partner or a resident director. That answer shapes everything after it. Check with the national regulator or a licensing adviser, because rules differ and change.

Ask the regulator for the application forms and the usual processing time before you commit to a lease. Offices differ in how they treat first-time applicants from abroad. A polite call early often saves weeks later. Keep a written record of every answer, because advice given verbally does not bind anyone.

Also check whether your visa or residency status affects your right to hold a licence or to be named as the responsible person on it.
Water and drains decide the site

A brewpub uses several litres of water for every litre of beer once cleaning is counted. It sends warm, sugary, high-strength effluent to the drain. Ask for the local water report before you sign anything. If the supply is very soft, very hard or desalinated, you will treat it. Treatment kit needs floor space. Our guide on water use per litre of beer gives you the figures to track from the first week.

Then ask the water utility what it will accept in the drain. Some cities set limits on temperature and pH. Some charge for load. Finding that out after the tanks are in is expensive.

One detail worth checking on a first site visit is the floor drain. A brewhouse sends wort, trub and cleaning chemicals down it. A drain that is too small or poorly sloped backs up at the worst moment, usually mid-cleaning. Run water through it and watch where it goes.

A brewhouse bought overseas arrives with a commissioning engineer for a few days, not for the life of the plant. Ask who will fix a pump motor or a control board in your country and how long a spare takes through customs. Keep a short list of consumables you cannot run without: gaskets, a spare pump seal, a temperature probe, sanitiser and cleaning chemicals.

Malt, hops and yeast may also come from far away. Plan stock for the longest lead time, not the average one. Store it cool.

Buy from a supplier that will share references from breweries in a similar climate. Voltage, frequency and gas type differ between countries, so confirm the plant matches your site's power before it ships. A wrong transformer can mean weeks of delay. Read importing brewing equipment for the freight and customs side.
The people you need before you open

You need a brewer who can run the plant unsupervised, a kitchen or food partner if your licence requires food, plus front-of-house staff who can describe your beers without a script. In a new country the hardest hire is often the brewer, so read brewpub or production brewery before you commit to a model that needs a full team on day one.

Work permits and local hiring rules apply to the brewer as much as to anyone. Ask early.

Do not assume local drinkers want the beers you love. Spend a month in the on-trade first: what people order, what they pay, what they eat with it and how long they stay. Local lagers and light ales usually sell the volume, with a few stronger or more unusual beers for the curious.

Plan the opening list around three or four beers that you can brew consistently. A small range brewed well beats a long menu brewed unevenly.

Talk to local bar and restaurant owners before you set prices. Pint size, glass shape and the habit of ordering by the bottle all differ. A pub that serves 330 ml bottles by habit will not sell a 568 ml pour easily. Our guide to pricing a pint in a brewpub shows how to work backwards from cost.

Regulators in most countries audit production volumes, stock and sales against the duty you pay. Start a simple log of brews, tank volumes, packaged volumes, losses and energy use. Logging brewery data you will use explains which fields earn their place and which are noise.

You will not know everything on opening day. A brewery that records what happened can learn from it. One that does not repeats the same mistakes. A tidy log also reassures lenders and regulators that the business is under control.
faqs: Do I need a local partner to open a brewpub abroad?
It depends on the country. Some require a resident director or a local shareholder for alcohol licences and some do not. Ask the national regulator or a licensing adviser before you form the company.
Should I bring a brewer with me or hire locally?

Either can work. A brewer you trust shortens the start-up, while a local hire knows the suppliers and the drinkers. Check work permit rules first. Plan a handover period if the first brewer will leave.
How much water will a brewpub use?
Plan for several litres of water per litre of beer once cleaning, cooling and rinsing are counted. Measure it from the first brew and track it weekly.

cta.title: Plan the business side before the brewhouse
cta.body: Brewery Business Management runs for three weeks and works through costing, pricing, licensing steps, forecasting and the figures a lender expects to see. Classes are live online on Saturdays and Sundays, 12:00 PM to 2:00 PM India Standard Time, so you join from your own time zone and recordings cover any class you miss. It teaches what a single guide cannot: how to put the numbers behind each decision.
